name: Forty Drafts of One Line
why_it_works: People trust craft they can see. Showing the bad drafts of one lyric before the final line proves the work and lets readers judge each version, and feeling smart about which line is better makes them invested in the finished song.

hook.pattern: Show the finished line crossed out with a big draft count, then promise to walk through how it got there.
examples: This one line took me {{draft_count}} drafts.
Draft one was flat. Draft {{draft_count}} made the song.
Which draft would you have kept?

variables.name: draft_count
variables.description: How many drafts it really took (a real number)

variables.name: middle_draft_number
variables.description: The real draft number of the middle draft shown

variables.name: draft_one
variables.description: An honest early, flat version of the line, capitalized
variables.example: I miss you when you're gone

variables.name: draft_two
variables.description: A better but still weak middle draft, capitalized
variables.example: The house is quiet since you left

variables.name: final_line
variables.description: The finished lyric line, capitalized, sung in one breath, 10 syllables or fewer
variables.example: Your cup still keeps the shape of morning

variables.name: key_object
variables.description: The concrete object at the center of the final line

variables.name: echo_words
variables.description: The words inside the final line that echo each other in sound

variables.name: listen_link
variables.description: Where to hear it, 4 words or fewer

slides.headline: {{draft_count}} drafts. One line.
slides.body: Swipe to watch a lyric get rewritten until it hurts right.
slides.visual_prompt: 4:5 photo of a messy notebook page full of crossed-out lines, desk lamp, coffee ring stain, top-down

slides.headline: Draft 1
slides.body: "{{draft_one}}". True, but you've heard it a thousand times.
slides.visual_prompt: Notebook close-up with the first line written then crossed out in red

slides.headline: Draft {{middle_draft_number}}
slides.body: "{{draft_two}}". Better. There's a picture now, but no surprise.
slides.visual_prompt: Close-up of a second line written neater, half crossed out, pencil resting on it

slides.headline: The rule that fixed it
slides.body: Show one object, not the feeling. Stress the object on the downbeat.
slides.visual_prompt: Single {{key_object}} on an empty table in morning window light, still life, 4:5

slides.headline: Draft {{draft_count}}
slides.visual_prompt: Clean handwritten final line on a fresh page, circled, soft morning light

slides.headline: Why it works
slides.body: Concrete object, internal echo ({{echo_words}}), and the key word lands on beat one.
slides.visual_prompt: Simple diagram slide: the lyric with stressed syllables in bold and beat numbers above

slides.headline: Hear it in the song
slides.visual_prompt: Cover-art end card, {{song_title}} title over a photo of the {{key_object}} in window light

cta: Hear the line in '{{song_title}}': {{listen_link}}. Which draft would you have kept?

craft.technique: Draft ladder (show the rewrite, teach the device)
craft.notes: The finished line should beat the drafts on three visible devices: a concrete image ({{key_object}}) instead of an abstract feeling, an internal echo (consonance or assonance inside the line, here {{echo_words}}), and the most important word on a stressed downbeat. Keep the final line singable in one breath, about 8-10 syllables. Spell the devices out on the 'Why it works' slide so readers learn something. Suggested tempo/feel if posted with audio: 70-80 BPM, solo acoustic guitar or piano, the final line sung once over the last slide.

do_not: Invent a fake draft count; use the real number or say 'dozens'
Quote or rewrite a famous song's lyric as the 'bad draft'
Make the drafts so bad they feel staged
